prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: inventory
Deck beneath it: Before any book is milled, every scanned volume on the shelf is graded by how hard its text will be to recover.

Hero: a tall bookshelf of old scanned volumes stands at the left, and from it one book at a time travels a bench of three examinations drawn across the middle of the page. At the first station, a caliper-like gauge rests on an open book and a tally card beside it reads: six pages sampled through the book — is the hidden text real words, or scanner noise? At the second station, a small desk telescope points out a window toward two distant buildings on a hill, labeled Internet Archive and Gutenberg, with a note: a cleaner text of the same book may already exist elsewhere; the nearer archive is asked first. At the third station, a hanging balance weighs the book and tips toward one of three bins.

Below the bench, the three bins stand in a row, drawn as open crates holding graded books: a full crate labeled easy — good text found, here or online; a half-full crate labeled medium; a sparse crate labeled hard — only the scanned pictures remain, with a small magnifier resting on a page of speckled unreadable type.

One quiet inset at the lower right: a book spine bearing a neat paper label in the form year, author, title, with a note — a book whose label breaks the pattern is flagged before it ever leaves the shelf.

The finished product leans at the far right: a single long ruled sheet titled the inventory, its rows drawn as small book spines ordered from a full-height easy group down to a short hard group.

One warm accent colour follows the graded books and the bins; the shelf, bench, and instruments stay in ink.
